title: What HIV does to the immune system
answer: Your immune system is your body's defence team against germs. HIV is a virus that attacks this defence team, especially special white blood cells called CD4 cells. It gets inside them, makes copies of itself and slowly destroys them. Over time, without treatment, the body loses so many CD4 cells that it struggles to fight even simple infections. The good news is that HIV treatment stops the virus from multiplying, so the immune system can stay strong and recover.

title: What CD4 cells are
answer: CD4 cells are a type of white blood cell that act like leaders of your immune system. They help the body recognise and fight germs. HIV targets these cells and destroys them. When a person takes HIV treatment well, the CD4 count usually goes up again. Your nurse or health worker can explain your own results.

title: How long it takes HIV to become AIDS
answer: Without treatment, HIV usually damages the immune system slowly, often over many years, before it reaches the most serious stage called AIDS. The time is different for each person. Some people get sick sooner than others. With HIV treatment taken every day, most people never develop AIDS and can live long, healthy lives. That is why testing early and starting treatment quickly is so important. If you are worried, talk to a nurse at your nearest health center.

title: The stages of HIV infection
answer: HIV has three main stages if it is not treated. First is acute infection, in the first weeks, when the virus multiplies fast and some people feel like they have flu. Second is the chronic or silent stage, which can last years; the person may feel fine, but the virus keeps damaging the immune system. Third is AIDS, when the immune system is badly damaged and serious illnesses appear. Treatment can stop HIV from moving through these stages.

title: Acute HIV infection in the first weeks
answer: Acute HIV infection is the first few weeks after the virus enters the body. During this time HIV multiplies very fast, so the amount of virus in the blood is high and it is easier to pass to others. Some people get flu-like signs such as fever, sore throat, rash, tiredness or swollen glands, usually for a short time. Many people feel nothing at all. If you had a recent risk, see a health worker for testing and advice.

title: Why symptoms cannot tell you if you have HIV
answer: You cannot know if you have HIV by checking how you feel. Early signs like fever, rash or sore throat are the same as many common illnesses such as flu or malaria, and many people with HIV have no signs at all for years. Feeling healthy does not mean you are HIV negative, and feeling sick does not mean you are positive. The only way to know is to take an HIV test at a health center or youth corner.

title: Signs of advanced HIV
answer: When HIV is not treated for a long time, the immune system becomes weak. Then a person may have signs such as losing a lot of weight, long-lasting fever, night sweats, diarrhoea that does not stop, a cough for weeks, or repeated infections. These signs can also come from other illnesses like TB, so they do not prove HIV. Anyone with these signs should go to a health center soon to be checked and tested.

title: What opportunistic infections are
answer: Opportunistic infections are illnesses that take the 'opportunity' to attack when the immune system is weak. A healthy immune system can usually control them, but untreated HIV can let them cause serious disease. Examples include TB, some types of pneumonia, fungal infections in the mouth, and some brain infections. Taking HIV treatment every day keeps the immune system strong and greatly lowers the chance of these illnesses. Health workers can also give medicines to prevent some of them.

title: Which body fluids can carry HIV
answer: HIV is found in enough amount to infect someone only in certain body fluids: blood, semen (cum), pre-cum, vaginal fluids, rectal (anal) fluids and breast milk. HIV is passed when one of these fluids from a person with HIV gets into another person's body, for example through sex without a condom, sharing needles, or from mother to baby. These fluids need to reach the bloodstream or a mucous membrane, like the inside of the vagina, anus, penis tip or mouth.

title: Body fluids that do not pass HIV
answer: Saliva (spit), tears, sweat, urine (pee) and faeces (poo) do not pass HIV, unless they have visible blood in them. These fluids do not carry enough virus to infect anyone. So you cannot get HIV from someone's sweat during sports, from their tears, from being spat on, or from sharing a toilet. HIV is passed only through blood, semen, pre-cum, vaginal fluids, anal fluids and breast milk.

title: Can HIV survive outside the body
answer: HIV is a weak virus outside the human body. It cannot live long in air, water or on surfaces, and it cannot multiply outside a person. That is why you cannot get HIV from door handles, clothes, bed sheets, toilet seats or water. The real risk comes from fresh blood or body fluids getting directly into your body, like through shared needles. If you have to clean up blood, use gloves or a plastic bag on your hands.

title: Why the body cannot clear HIV by itself
answer: Many germs like flu are cleared by the immune system after some days. HIV is different. It hides inside immune cells and puts its own genetic material into them, so the body cannot fully remove it. This is why HIV stays for life. Treatment cannot remove it either, but it keeps the virus asleep and very low so the person stays healthy. This is also why HIV must be prevented and why treatment must be taken every day.

answer: Yes. HIV can affect anyone of any age, including teenagers and young adults. title: Blood contact during sports and fights
answer: The risk of HIV from blood contact during sports or a fight is extremely low. HIV can only pass if fresh blood from a person with HIV gets directly into an open wound or into your eyes or mouth. If there is bleeding, stop playing, cover the wound, clean blood with gloves or a barrier, and wash with soap and water. If you are worried about a big blood exposure, talk to a health worker.
